9
The velocity–time graphs of four different objects are shown.
Which graph represents an object falling from rest through a long distance in the Earth’s
atmosphere?
A
B
velocity
velocity
0
0
time
0

D
velocity

hints: Notice the wording from rest and long distance: the velocity-time graph must start at $0$ and have time to level off at a maximum velocity.
Remember the gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, and air drag grows as velocity grows.
Check which graph starts steep with acceleration near $g$ and then flattens as drag approaches weight and resultant acceleration approaches zero.
walkthrough: Identify the conditions: initial velocity $v = 0$ at $t = 0$, and a long fall in air means drag cannot be ignored and terminal velocity can be reached.

Use the graph rule: gradient of velocity-time equals acceleration. Initially $v = 0$ so drag is zero and resultant acceleration is maximum, about $g$, so the curve starts at the origin with a steep slope.
Apply the drag argument: as $v$ increases, upward drag increases, so resultant force $F = mg - \text{drag}$ decreases and acceleration decreases, so the gradient must get smaller.
For a long fall, drag eventually equals weight, resultant force is zero and acceleration is zero, so velocity becomes constant at terminal velocity and the graph becomes horizontal.
Only the curve that starts at $(0,0)$, has decreasing gradient, and levels to a plateau matches this cause-and-effect chain. This is option D.

A.explanation: Straight line from the origin means constant gradient and so constant acceleration, which is fall in vacuum with no air resistance.

B.explanation: Horizontal line starting above zero means constant non-zero velocity from $t = 0$, so it does not start from rest.

C.explanation: Curve with increasing gradient means acceleration is increasing, whereas air resistance makes resultant force and acceleration decrease as velocity grows.

D.explanation: Curve starts at zero with large gradient that decreases to zero, showing acceleration falling to zero as the object approaches terminal velocity.
